prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
When you type an address such as https://www.example.com/articles/42 into a browser and press Enter, the browser first splits it into parts. The scheme is https, the host is www.example.com, the port is 443 because none was given, and the path is /articles/42. Before it uses the network, the browser checks local sources. It looks in its HTTP cache for a stored copy of the page that is still fresh, and if it finds one it can show the page with no request at all. It checks whether a service worker registered for that site wants to handle the request. It also consults its HSTS list, which records hosts that must only be reached over HTTPS, and this matters most when a person has typed http:// or the bare host name.

Next, the browser needs an IP address for the host name, because the network routes packets by address. It looks in its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system, which keeps a cache of its own and reads the local hosts file. If neither has the answer, the operating system sends a query to a recursive resolver. This is usually run by the internet provider or by a public service such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8, and the address of the resolver is set on the machine or handed out by the router. The query normally travels over UDP to port 53. Some browsers send it over HTTPS to the resolver instead, so that the local network cannot read it.

The resolver may have the answer cached, in which case it replies within a few milliseconds. If it does not, it works down the DNS hierarchy. It asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks one of those which servers are responsible for example.com, and asks one of those, called the authoritative servers, for the address of www.example.com. The reply carries a time to live, commonly between 60 and 3,600 seconds, which tells each cache along the way how long it may keep the answer. The site may return an IPv4 address in an A record, an IPv6 address in an AAAA record, or both. When both exist, the browser tries IPv6 first and starts on IPv4 as well if there is no connection after about 250 milliseconds, then keeps whichever connects first. A full lookup with nothing cached commonly takes between 20 and 120 milliseconds.

With an address in hand, the browser opens a connection. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 this is a TCP connection, which begins with a three-step handshake. The browser sends a SYN packet, the server answers with SYN-ACK, and the browser replies with ACK. The browser can send data from that point, so the handshake costs one round trip between the two machines. A round trip to a server on the same continent is often 20 to 50 milliseconds, and to the far side of the world it can pass 250. If the browser has learned from an earlier visit that the server supports HTTP/3, it may use QUIC instead. QUIC runs over UDP and combines the transport and encryption handshakes into one.

On a TCP connection the TLS handshake follows. The browser sends a ClientHello message that lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, a random value and a key share for the key exchange. It includes the host name in a field called Server Name Indication, so that a server hosting many sites on one address knows which certificate to present. It also lists the application protocols it speaks, such as h2 and http/1.1, in an extension called ALPN. In TLS 1.3 the server replies with its own key share, which lets both sides work out the same session keys, and everything after that point is encrypted. The server then sends its certificate, a signature that proves it holds the matching private key, and a Finished message. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for this. TLS 1.2 needs two, which is one reason operators move servers to the newer version.

The browser checks the certificate before it trusts anything the server says. It confirms that the certificate names www.example.com and that today's date falls inside its validity period, which for public certificates is now at most 398 days. It confirms that a chain of signatures leads from the server's certificate, through one or more intermediate certificates, to a root certificate already installed in the browser or operating system. It also looks for signed certificate transparency records, and it may check for revocation using a stapled OCSP response from the server or a revocation list that the browser keeps. If any check fails, the browser shows a warning page and does not send the request.

Once the handshake is finished, the browser sends the HTTP request through the encrypted channel. In HTTP/2 this is a set of binary frames with compressed headers, but in readable form it is a request line, GET /articles/42, followed by headers. The Host header, or the :authority field in HTTP/2, names www.example.com. The browser adds its User-Agent, the content types it accepts, a header saying it can decompress gzip and br, and any cookies stored for that site. Cookies make the request larger, and they go only to the host that set them.

The request reaches the server, though not always the machine the browser might picture. Many sites sit behind a content delivery network or a load balancer. The address from DNS leads to an edge server near the user, which ends the TLS connection and either answers from its own cache or forwards the request to an origin server over a separate connection. If the response has to be built, the origin application matches the path to a handler, which may query a database, call other services and render HTML. Each of those steps adds time before anything can be sent back.

The server then writes a status line and headers, such as 200 OK and Content-Type: text/html, and begins sending the body. The moment the first byte of that response reaches the browser is called time to first byte, and it is the end of the period described here. It covers the DNS lookup, the TCP and TLS handshakes, the travel of the request to the server, the server's own work and the first part of the response's journey back. A warm connection to a nearby server can show a time to first byte under 100 milliseconds, and a cold connection to a distant server with a slow application can take over a second. In my view the useful lesson for a developer is that most of the early steps depend on distance and round trips and not on bandwidth. Reusing connections, caching DNS answers and responses, and keeping certificate chains short will usually do more at this stage than making files smaller.
